Metal Finishing Rinse Control Decisions | AquaMesh Platform How it works Case studies Company Book a demo Manufacturing Field note · Metal finishing · September 30, 2026 Start with what the rinse loop already knows. A finishing line can have a good conductivity controller and still lack a clear account of which production change increased water use or sent more chemistry toward treatment. The first job is to join the evidence already there. This is a proposed operating study, not a measured AquaMesh result at a metal finishing plant. What is established Conductivity control has a real job. An EPA Region 9 metal finishing project describes the basic rinse loop: a conductivity sensor and analyzer open a solenoid valve when the rinse reaches a set point, then close it after the reading falls below a deadband. The goal is adequate rinsing without constant fresh water flow. The same report recommends tracking set points, bath conditions and rejected parts when adjusting the system. The EPA example predates today's software, but its control principle matters. A new platform should not pretend that water savings begin with a novel probe if a conductivity controller, countercurrent rinse or dragout reduction can already address the problem. EPA's pollution prevention manual also describes flow restriction, pH and conductivity control, and dragout reduction as established options. What changed this week Modern automation makes the existing evidence easier to use. In a September 28, 2026 WEFTEC announcement , Schneider Electric described upgrades across PLC security, open automation, connected data and water management software. Schneider says its EcoStruxure Water Advisor and AVEVA CONNECT offerings bring together operational data and analytics. Those are substantial incumbent capabilities. An AquaMesh proposal has to begin by documenting what the facility's PLC, SCADA, historian, water treatment program and service provider already cover. For a rinse line, the missing question may be operational rather than computational: when conductivity rises, was it the expected result of a particular rack, bath concentration or changeover, a valve problem, a drifted probe, or a genuine process upset? A conductivity trend alone cannot distinguish all of those causes. That is a hypothesis to test at the facility, not a claim that a named vendor's system cannot solve it. A practical test Follow one event from part to treatment. 1 Define the decision Choose one rinse tank and one action the shift team can approve: inspect a valve, check a probe, adjust a set point within a qualified window, change a dragout practice, or hold a batch for quality review. Keep product quality and discharge requirements as hard constraints. 2 Align existing timestamps Put rack or barrel movements, bath condition, conductivity, valve state, makeup flow, reject records and wastewater treatment data on the same timeline. Separate normal load changes from events that would justify intervention. The EPA metal finishing project specifically ties set point review to bath condition and rejects; that is the starting evidence, not an optional afterthought. 3 State what remains unknown If installed measurements show a change but cannot identify the physical condition needed for the chosen decision, define the missing variable and sampling location. Test any proposed optical measurement against a relevant laboratory method across real bath and rinse conditions. Do not infer a metal concentration, compliance result or validated spectral performance from an uncalibrated signal. 4 Verify the response After an operator approved action, check rinse conductivity and flow alongside part quality and downstream treatment evidence. A lower water reading alone is not a win if it increases rejects or dragin to the next bath. AquaMesh's proposed role is to connect the event, likely cause, authorized action and verification. The installed controller still performs its control duty; new sensing has to earn its place through a defined comparison. Sources and scope Opened primary sources. U.S. EPA Region 9, Reducing Rinse Water Use With Conductivity Control Systems , December 1996. Describes the control loop and a facility evaluation; historical evidence, not a claim about current installations. U.S. EPA, Pollution Prevention for the Metal Finishing Industry , rinse water and dragout control guidance. Schneider Electric, WEFTEC 2026 announcement , September 28, 2026. Vendor description of its own automation and software scope. The event study and proposed AquaMesh workflow above are inference. No customer savings, sensor accuracy or vendor gap is asserted. Find the rinse decision your data cannot explain. Start with the controller and process records already in use, then validate any remaining measurement gap. Industrial Water Reuse Monitoring Guide | AquaMesh Platform How it works Case studies Company Book a demo Industrial water Field note · Industrial water reuse · September 29, 2026 Match the signal to the failure you need to catch. A reuse line can have plenty of measurements and still leave an operator without an answer. The starting question is specific: which developing condition would change a routing, treatment or maintenance decision while there is still time to act? This is an operating framework, not a report of AquaMesh performance at a customer site. Requirements vary with water source, end use and permit. Start with the use One reuse system, several different questions. A flow balance can show that recovered water is being produced without reaching a use point. It cannot establish that the water is suitable for that use. A quality reading at the treatment outlet can show a process change, but it does not identify which valve or demand change caused a routing loss. The operator needs both views on the same timeline. The end use sets the required treatment and monitoring context. As one example, EPA’s September 2026 summary of California rules for recycled municipal wastewater distinguishes industrial cooling that creates mist from cooling that does not; its table also identifies continuous turbidity monitoring for certain disinfected tertiary uses and separate coliform sampling. That state-specific summary is not a universal specification for every industrial process water loop. EPA: California industrial reuse summary . Choose the evidence What does each measurement actually establish? 1 Flow, level and valve state Use these with production and demand records to locate a water balance or routing problem. Check meter health and whether measurements represent the same operating interval before calling the difference a loss. 2 Pressure and turbidity Use treatment equipment status and appropriate quality tags to flag a filtration change. An alarm should point to the affected train, its operating mode and the approved response. A turbidity signal is not a direct microbial measurement. 3 Laboratory and microbiological evidence Keep the prescribed sampling and methods authoritative. A 2026 Water Research Foundation project tested automated ATP monitoring at a full-scale non-potable reuse facility during normal operation and simulated treatment failures. Its public abstract reports detection of simulated membrane failures within minutes and describes ATP as a complement to conventional laboratory monitoring. That result is evidence for the studied application, not validation of an optical probe or a substitute for a site’s compliance method. WRF project 5319 . 4 Composition at a decision point If the available tags show that a stream changed but cannot distinguish the physical condition that determines whether it can be reused, define that gap precisely. A targeted spectral measurement might be tested for a suitable chemical or organic signature, with paired laboratory samples, a defined range, fouling checks and false-alarm review. It must not be presented as a pathogen test or as a validated concentration before that validation exists. A testable operating study Work backward from the decision. For a hypothetical reuse train, pick one event that would trigger a hold, diversion, inspection or return to service under the plant’s own procedures. Reconstruct the event using timestamped SCADA and historian tags, equipment and maintenance records, production demand, and the laboratory sample collection and result times. Include normal runs for comparison. At each point, write down what the operator knew then , not what became clear days later. Test whether the existing instruments give enough warning and a likely cause. If they do, improve the decision route and verification. If they do not, specify the missing physical observation and test a sensor at that location. Route any proposed response for operator approval, then check the downstream trend and reference sample against the expected result. A useful alert names the condition, evidence, owner and action window. The measurement earns its place when it improves that decision and the result can be checked. Sources and scope Primary sources. U.S. EPA, California industrial reuse summary , updated September 9, 2026. This summarizes state rules and directs readers to the state for current requirements. The Water Research Foundation, project 5319 , report dated July 21, 2026. This article uses the public project abstract; the full report requires subscriber access. The sequence of decisions and the hypothetical study above are AquaMesh’s interpretation. No customer outcome or sensor performance is asserted. Find the decision your plant cannot make soon enough. AquaMesh starts with existing plant data and adds sensing where a specific visibility gap remains. Liquid Cooling Water Quality Decisions | AquaMesh Platform How it works Case studies Company Book a demo Data centers Field note · Liquid cooling · September 29, 2026 Separate the loop before the alarm. A water quality alert has little value until the team knows which cooling circuit it describes, who owns that circuit, and what action the evidence supports. This is an operating framework based on published guidance, not a report of AquaMesh performance at a data center. First boundary Facility water and server coolant are different systems. An ASHRAE TC 9.9 white paper distinguishes facility water systems (FWS) from technology cooling systems (TCS), which a coolant distribution unit commonly separates. The paper warns that applying the quality specification for one loop to the other can either impose needless cost on the facility side or leave the IT side at risk. It also notes that ownership may differ between facilities staff, the IT owner, equipment provider and service provider. Before setting a threshold, draw that boundary on the plant diagram. Identify the sample point, fluid, treatment program, materials, control owner and equipment manufacturer's requirements. A signal on a cooling tower does not establish the condition inside a separated server loop. Nor does a server-side result alone identify a tower fault. Existing coverage Use each signal for the question it answers. 1 Thermal and hydraulic tags Trend supply and return temperature, flow, pressure differential, pump and valve state, filter differential pressure, and load by operating mode. These records can localize a heat transfer or flow problem. They do not, by themselves, identify its chemical cause. The Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory liquid cooling controls guide describes the data inputs and ownership choices involved. 2 Conductivity, pH and turbidity ASHRAE describes these as an intermediate online monitoring option, with cost and risk determining whether it is warranted. Conductivity responds to dissolved ionic content; it is not a specific contaminant assay. The USGS conductance reference explains that the reading depends on the types and amounts of dissolved substances and temperature. Interpret a change alongside makeup water, dosing, temperature compensation and the correct loop's specification. 3 Samples and equipment guidance Maintain the sampling and analysis required by the fluid and equipment providers. ASHRAE's paper calls for a monitoring frequency and an agreed response to out-of-range values; it explicitly retains periodic bacteria samples. A conductivity, pH or turbidity trend does not replace those tests or prove biological safety. 4 A defined missing observation If existing tags flag a change but cannot distinguish the physical state that would change an operator decision, write down that missing variable and the point of measurement. Targeted spectral sensing could be evaluated for a suitable signature with paired reference samples, interference and fouling checks, and false-alarm review. No spectral result should be treated as a validated concentration, bacteria test or corrosion-rate measurement without application-specific validation. Operating test Reconstruct the decision at the time it mattered. Choose one historical water quality or cooling event. Align the existing BMS or historian trends with lab sample collection time, dosing and maintenance records, operating mode, and CDU status. Ask which loop changed first, whether the evidence identified a likely cause, and who had authority to isolate, sample, inspect or hold equipment under the site's procedures. Compare with a normal run before declaring an anomaly. Then define a prospective test: a condition that triggers an operator-reviewed action, an acceptable false-alarm rate, and the downstream signal or sample that would verify the response. ASHRAE emphasizes an agreed plan for out-of-range results; this is where monitoring becomes a decision rather than another chart. Start with the loop, the owner and the response window. Add an instrument only when the evidence required for that decision is missing from the installed controls and sampling program. Sources and scope Primary references. ASHRAE TC 9.9, Water-Cooled Servers: Common Designs, Components, and Processes , especially water quality and monitoring sections. Published guidance, not an AquaMesh validation. U.S. Geological Survey, Specific Electrical Conductance , measurement basis for conductivity. Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Liquid Cooling Controls Team white paper , control system data inputs. The historical review and prospective test are AquaMesh's proposed method. They are not a claim of a particular site's results or a tested AquaSpectra performance level. Find the decision your cooling data cannot make soon enough. AquaMesh starts with installed controls and samples, then tests sensing against a specific visibility gap. TITLE: UV/Vis Spectral Sensing and AI for Industrial Water
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/insights/spectral-sensing-ai-industrial-water.html
DATE: 
SECTION: Insights
==============================================================================

UV/Vis Spectral Sensing and AI for Industrial Water | AquaMesh Platform How it works Case studies Company Book a demo Technical guide · Process measurement · 7 October 2026 How spectral sensing and AI work together in industrial water. Spectral instruments can reveal a change in a process stream. SCADA, production records and lab results explain what the plant was doing when it happened. An operational model becomes useful when it joins those two views and gives an operator a testable decision. Engineering framework, not a report of a validated AquaMesh industrial sensor deployment or customer savings. Site-specific testing is required before treating any optical estimate as a calibrated parameter. Direct answer What does combining spectroscopy with AI actually do? UV/Vis spectroscopy and AI serve different roles. A spectral instrument records wavelength-dependent light absorption in a sample or process stream. Depending on the instrument and application, that signal may reveal changes in dissolved constituents or suspended material. The process model combines the optical signal with existing data such as flows, valve states, batch changes, conductivity, temperatures, and laboratory samples. It then tests likely causes, estimates an operating consequence, routes a recommendation to an operator, and checks the subsequent result. It does not automatically identify every chemical, produce a regulatory BOD or COD measurement, or prove that a process change caused a loss. The physical measurement, model and operational decision each need separate validation. For a plant that already has sufficient instruments, the right starting point is historian and SCADA analysis . Additional spectral sensing only makes sense when an existing measurement cannot resolve a valuable decision. How it works Five steps from water measurement to operating action. 1 Locate the loss or unstable condition Pick one operating question, such as product carryover during a cleaning transition or unexpected organic loading. Define which action would change if the condition were detected earlier. 2 Use existing tags before adding hardware Align historian, PLC, SCADA, production, maintenance and laboratory timestamps. Check units, sensor faults, equipment operating modes, and whether the signal already answers the question. 3 Measure a missing physical signal If ordinary conductivity, flow or sample data cannot distinguish product from rinse water, evaluate UV/Vis absorbance or another appropriate optical method at the decision point. NIR or Raman may be useful for different materials, but each has its own optical and deployment constraints. 4 Connect a change to its process context Compare the spectrum or derived indicator with recipe, changeover, valve and flow records. Rank plausible causes; quantify the opportunity using the site's own throughput, unit values and tariffs. Flag uncertainty instead of presenting a correlation as a diagnosis. 5 Verify an operator-approved response Present the evidence and proposed check to the responsible operator. After a permitted adjustment, compare the subsequent physical reading and production outcome against the expected result. Preserve an audit trail, including rejected recommendations. Two applications Where the combination matters. Food and beverage: product loss and clean-in-place (CIP) transitions Suppose a dairy or beverage plant changes from product to rinse water. The plant's PLC shows the changeover and routing valve, but a time-based recipe does not directly establish when the remaining product has cleared the line. A suitably validated optical trend at a return or drain point could be correlated with the valve sequence to test a narrower diversion interval. The analysis must distinguish product variation, entrained air, suspended particles, sensor fouling and cleaning chemistry before recommending a change. Financial value combines demonstrably recoverable product, water, energy and treatment charges, net of implementation cost. Industrial wastewater: unexpected organic load or treatment upset An optical trend may provide earlier evidence that the incoming water has changed than a delayed grab-sample result. Flow, tank levels, upstream production and aeration records help establish whether the change is operationally important and where it originated. A trend is not a certified BOD or COD result: site-specific paired samples, error bounds and the required reference method remain authoritative for compliance. Read more about spectral change detection versus calibrated parameters . Validation What must be proved before a plant relies on it? Instrument: establish the optical range and field stability, inspect fouling, scattering, bubbles, temperature effects and matrix variation; verify cleaning and maintenance intervals. Model: keep entire batches, recipes and operating periods out of training, then measure false alarms, missed events, drift and error against independently timed reference observations. Operating decision: show that an alert arrived before a real decision window closed, its suggested cause was investigated, and the action and result were independently verified. For BOD or COD estimation, do not inherit a vendor's generic calibration as proof for an unfamiliar effluent. In a six-plant study archived by EPA, wastewater-specific calibration improved the accuracy of UV/Vis estimates relative to broader models. USGS field guidance on fluorescence sensors, a related but distinct optical measurement method, also documents interference, maintenance and quality-control requirements. A laboratory result remains authoritative wherever the permit or approved procedure requires it. The purchase test is a decision, not a dashboard. If an existing historian tag reliably supports the same action, adding a spectral instrument is not justified. If the missing measurement changes an economically important decision, define the blind test and the maximum acceptable error before ordering hardware. Common questions Frequently asked engineering questions. Can UV/Vis spectroscopy measure BOD and COD directly? No. The instrument measures optical response. BOD and COD may be estimated through calibrated surrogate models for a particular water matrix. Performance can change with suspended particles, composition and operating conditions. Reference laboratory methods are still needed for calibration and any legally required reporting. Does a plant need an additional sensor to use AI optimization? Not necessarily. Much of the initial value can come from existing historian, SCADA, production and lab records. Add instrumentation only where a clear measurement gap prevents a consequential operating decision. How is this different from a conventional water quality dashboard? A dashboard reports instrument values and alarms. The proposed process model connects a developing condition to equipment state, likely causes, operational consequences, a named operator response and subsequent verification. The difference must be tested on real operating evidence rather than inferred from the interface. Does AquaMesh replace PLCs, SCADA or laboratory reporting? No. AquaMesh is designed as an advisory layer alongside existing controls and reference methods. The first step is read-only analysis; any future control integration must be separately approved and validated by the plant. References and scope Independent technical sources. Rieger, Langergraber Siegrist, Water Science and Technology (2006), indexed by U.S. EPA : UV/Vis wastewater calibration study; establishes the importance of wastewater-specific calibration. Water Research (2016), calibration of UV/Vis spectrophotometers : compares calibration approaches and model performance for TSS and COD estimation in sewers, treatment plants and rivers. U.S. Geological Survey, Techniques and Methods 1-D11 : optical instrument selection, interference, cleaning and quality assurance for fluorescence measurements. U.S. Geological Survey, Open-File Report 2026-1063 : turbidity corrections and verification considerations for fluorescent dissolved organic matter (fDOM) sensors. These sources support general measurement cautions; they are not independent validation of AquaSpectra or AquaMesh. AquaMesh's industrial spectral instrument and any site-specific BOD model require validation before performance claims can be made. Start with a decision your plant cannot make soon enough. We can examine the process, existing records and the cost of that blind spot before deciding whether optical sensing is needed. TITLE: Intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal: what DO sensor precision actually controls
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/intermittent-aeration-nitrogen-removal-do-control.html
DATE: 2026-10-23
SECTION: Field notes
TAGS: nitrogen removal, intermittent aeration, dissolved oxygen, SND, wastewater treatment
==============================================================================

Biological nitrogen removal is one of the more demanding process control challenges in activated sludge treatment. Plants with tight effluent nitrogen limits need to run two competing biological processes: nitrification under aerobic conditions and denitrification under anoxic ones, efficiently, in the same biological system. For plants using intermittent aeration to accomplish this in a single-basin configuration, the precision of dissolved oxygen control during aeration cycles is not an instrumentation detail. It is the variable that determines whether the strategy works.

## What intermittent aeration is trying to do

Conventional biological nitrogen removal stages aerobic and anoxic zones in sequence: ammonia is nitrified to nitrate in an aerated zone, then denitrified to nitrogen gas in a downstream anoxic zone. The system is reliable but capital-intensive and requires careful hydraulic design.

Intermittent aeration takes a different path: the same basin alternates between aerobic and anoxic phases by cycling blowers on and off. During the aerated phase, nitrifiers convert ammonia to nitrate. During the unaerated phase, denitrifiers reduce nitrate to nitrogen gas, using carbon already present in the mixed liquor. Some organisms can carry out both reactions near-simultaneously at low dissolved oxygen concentrations, a phenomenon called simultaneous nitrification-denitrification (SND). The EPA Nutrient Control Design Manual identifies low-DO operation, typically below 1.0 mg/L, as a condition that promotes SND in conventional activated sludge by creating anoxic microsites within biological flocs. ([EPA, Nutrient Control Design Manual, 2010, Section 5](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2019-08/documents/nutrient-control-design-manual.pdf))

A 2022 review in Chemical Engineering Journal analyzed over 50 intermittent aeration studies and found that precise DO control during aeration phases was the most consistent predictor of nitrogen removal efficiency, ahead of cycle length or influent carbon-to-nitrogen ratio. ([Miao et al., 2022, Chemical Engineering Journal, doi:10.1016/j.cej.2021.133516](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S1385894721047604))

The practical appeal is real: intermittent aeration can achieve substantial nitrogen removal without a separate anoxic zone, with lower aeration energy than continuous-aeration systems, and with flexible response to variable influent loads. These advantages depend on cycle timing, and cycle timing depends on DO measurement.

## Where DO control precision comes in

The cycle timing in intermittent aeration is almost always governed by a dissolved oxygen setpoint rather than a fixed timer. Aeration turns on when DO falls below a lower bound; it turns off when DO rises above an upper bound. The accuracy of that DO band controls the effectiveness of the strategy:

**Sensor reading low (common fouling failure):** A sensor that reads 0.4 mg/L when actual DO is 1.8 mg/L keeps blowers running long past the point where nitrification has completed. The aerobic phase extends beyond the design intent. The anoxic fraction shrinks. Denitrification suffers, nitrogen removal drops, and the plant uses more electricity than the intermittent strategy was supposed to require.

**Sensor reading high:** Aeration shuts off early. The basin does not complete nitrification in one cycle. Ammonia carries over. In a plant with a permit nitrogen limit, this is an effluent compliance risk, not just an energy problem.

**Fouling that accumulates between cycles:** Mixed liquor accumulates on membrane or optical sensor surfaces during the unaerated phase. When aeration restarts, the sensor enters the aerobic phase with an offset that compounds over successive cycles if cleaning intervals are not calibrated to match actual fouling rates.

The cumulative effect is that the DO setpoints operators specify on the control screen may not correspond to the dissolved oxygen concentration the organisms experience. The blower control loop optimizes against a sensor output, not against the process state.

## What this looks like in practice

The same phenomenon described in the parallel-basin aeration analysis applies here in a temporal rather than spatial dimension. In that case, two basins running simultaneously showed a DO divergence that reflected sensor drift rather than process differences: one blower was pinned at maximum output, consuming over $3,000 per year more than its twin, for the full 25-day record. The spatial version was visible by comparing basins side by side. The parallel equipment drift analysis is in [why parallel equipment drifts apart](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts/), and the full historian data methodology is in [what 25 days of historian data actually shows about a treatment plant](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows/).

The temporal version in intermittent aeration requires a different analysis: charting DO sensor output against blower on/off timestamps at five-minute or finer resolution, and comparing aerobic phase duration over time. A sensor reading accurately produces aerobic phases of consistent duration for a given influent load. A sensor that is drifting produces phases that systematically lengthen (reading low, blowers run long) or shorten (reading high, blowers cut off early) in ways that do not track influent load changes.

Both versions share the same root cause: the measurement feeding the control loop has an offset that the loop cannot self-detect, because there is no independent reference running alongside it.

## The energy calculation for intermittent aeration

The aeration energy baseline for secondary treatment, around 1,500 kWh per million gallons for activated sludge, assumes reasonably continuous aeration. Intermittent aeration in a nitrogen-removal configuration typically aims to reduce aeration runtime to 50 to 70 percent of total time, depending on the carbon-to-nitrogen ratio of the influent and the cycle design. That would imply aeration energy in the range of 750 to 1,050 kWh per million gallons when timing is accurate.

At a 10 MGD plant and the current EIA industrial rate of $0.0977 per kWh ([EIA Electric Power Monthly, September 2026](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_5_6_a)), the difference between accurate intermittent aeration (approximately 900 kWh/MG as a midpoint) and sensor-extended aeration (1,500 kWh/MG because the sensor is holding blowers on too long) is approximately $215,000 per year at that scale.

**Modelled example for a 10 MGD plant with intermittent aeration:**

| | Accurate DO control | DO sensor drifting low |
|---|---|---|
| Aeration runtime share | 60% | 100% (effectively continuous) |
| Estimated kWh/MG | 900 | 1,500 |
| Annual energy cost at $0.098/kWh | $193,100 | $321,900 |
| Annual cost difference | | $128,800 |

This is a modelled example using published benchmarks; actual values depend on plant-specific loading, cycle design, and the degree of sensor offset. The direction is consistent: sensor drift in an intermittent aeration system does not only affect nitrogen removal performance. It erodes the energy savings that justified the intermittent strategy in the first place.

## What accurate DO measurement enables

When DO measurement in an intermittent aeration system is continuous, accurate, and corrected against drift between calibration intervals, the control loop can do what it was designed for: maintain the aerobic-to-anoxic balance that both nitrification and denitrification require.

For plants approaching permit limits on total nitrogen, the margin for process error is narrow. A sensor that introduces a systematic offset into the timing of aeration cycles is a measurement problem that manifests as an effluent compliance risk. The issue is usually visible in the historian data before it appears in the permit reporting: aerobic phase durations extending over time, DO baseline at cycle start gradually increasing, nitrogen removal efficiency declining in ways that do not correlate with influent load.

The diagnostic questions are the same ones that apply to continuous aeration systems. Are the DO sensors reading accurately between calibrations? Does blower runtime at a given influent load match what the setpoints predict? Are cycle times stable, or are they drifting? The methodology for that analysis is in [aeration energy at wastewater plants: the cost, the waste, and the measurement gap](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/aeration-energy-cost-wastewater-plants/).

None of this analysis requires new hardware. The data is in the historian. The constraint is having a way to extract it at the resolution that shows cycle-level behavior, over a long enough window, against a reference that was not subject to the same drift.

---

If your plant uses intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal and you want to understand whether your DO control is performing as designed, the place to start is the cycle data already in your historian.

See what that review looked like at an operating plant: [a membrane-bioreactor water reuse plant case study](https://aquamesh.ai/case-studies/water-reuse-plant.html). Or [reach out to schedule a working session with the team](https://aquamesh.ai/#contact).

*Alex Towfigh is a founder at AquaMesh.*

TITLE: Data center WUE: what the metric measures, what it misses, and what it takes to move it
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/data-center-wue-measurement-gap.html
DATE: 2026-10-22
SECTION: Measurement
TAGS: data centers, WUE, water efficiency, cooling tower, water monitoring, water usage effectiveness
==============================================================================

Water Usage Effectiveness, or WUE, has become the standard headline number for data center water efficiency. It is reported in sustainability disclosures, cited in regulatory proceedings, and used in site-selection discussions in water-stressed regions. The formula is simple: liters of water consumed at a facility divided by kilowatt-hours delivered to IT equipment.

What WUE does not tell you is where the water is going, what is controlling it in real time, or whether the sensors responsible for that control are working. That is a separate question, and the answer to it determines whether a WUE target is achievable or theoretical.

## What WUE actually measures

The metric was introduced by The Green Grid, the data center industry consortium, as a companion to PUE (Power Usage Effectiveness). Like PUE, it is a ratio: lower is better and zero is the theoretical ideal. A site with a WUE of 2.0 consumes two liters of water for every kilowatt-hour its servers use.

Research on actual facility performance puts the range between 1 and 9 liters per kilowatt-hour depending on cooling approach, climate zone, and facility age, with a central tendency around 1.5 to 2 L/kWh for older evaporative cooling installations. ([Mytton, D. "Data centre water consumption." npj Clean Water 4, 52 (2021)](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41545-021-00101-w)) Newer hyperscale builds using advanced chemistry management or closed-loop cooling report considerably lower values.

WUE is typically calculated annually. Some operators report quarterly. It is a useful benchmark for comparing facilities against each other and tracking long-run progress. It is a poor guide for what to do on Tuesday.

## Where the water actually goes

For facilities using evaporative cooling towers, which covers the majority of installed capacity, the water balance has two main terms: evaporation and blowdown.

Evaporation is the productive part. The cooling process works by letting water absorb heat and leave the tower as vapor. Roughly 70 to 80 percent of the water that enters the tower in this way is not recoverable; it has done its job and left the site. ([Mytton 2021](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41545-021-00101-w)) This fraction tracks the heat load on the facility and varies with ambient wet-bulb temperature. A site cannot significantly reduce evaporative losses without changing the physics of how it cools its equipment.

Blowdown is different. As water circulates through the tower and a portion evaporates, the dissolved minerals left behind concentrate. Calcium, silica, chlorides, and biological material accumulate. If concentration rises too high, scale deposits on heat exchanger surfaces and corrosion accelerates. To prevent this, some fraction of the circulating water is periodically discharged and replaced with fresh makeup water. That discharge is blowdown.

The ratio of dissolved mineral concentration in the circulating water to the concentration in the makeup supply is called the cycles of concentration. At three cycles, for every gallon that evaporates, roughly half a gallon is discharged as blowdown, and one and a half gallons are drawn in as makeup. At six cycles, blowdown drops to roughly one fifth of the evaporation volume. At ten cycles, it drops to one ninth.

**Modelled example:** For a 10-megawatt IT load facility with a moderate WUE of 2.0 L/kWh operating at 85 percent utilization, annual water consumption is roughly 149 million liters. If evaporation represents 75 percent of that total, the remaining 37 million liters per year is blowdown. Moving from 3 to 6 cycles of concentration reduces that blowdown component by approximately 60 percent, or 22 million liters per year. This is a modelled estimate based on the ratios above; actual results depend on makeup water chemistry, heat load profile, and seasonal variation.

## The measurement problem

The control system that manages blowdown uses a conductivity sensor as its primary input. Conductivity in the circulating water rises as dissolved minerals concentrate, and the controller uses this as a proxy for cycles of concentration. When conductivity reaches a set threshold, the blowdown valve opens and makeup water flows in.

This means the conductivity sensor, sitting in a basin or on a sidestream line, is the direct operational driver of water efficiency performance. A sensor that reads accurately and holds its calibration enables tight control at higher cycles. A sensor that has fouled, drifted, or been calibrated infrequently has the opposite effect.

A sensor reading low when concentration is actually high causes the controller to keep the blowdown valve closed longer than intended. Dissolved solids accumulate beyond design limits. Scale risk increases and the operator may not know it until a heat exchanger inspection. A sensor reading high when concentration is actually normal causes the controller to open the blowdown valve prematurely and repeatedly, discharging good water and drawing in fresh makeup water unnecessarily. The facility's WUE is higher than it needs to be, and the cause does not appear in the annual report.

Neither failure mode triggers an alarm in a standard building management system. The control loop is running. The conductivity reading is within the operating range. The controller is doing exactly what it was programmed to do with the signal it receives.

This is the same silent failure pattern that affects dissolved oxygen control in wastewater aeration basins, where a fouled sensor drives blowers toward wasted energy rather than toward needed oxygen. The structure of the problem is identical: a lagging indicator (WUE for water, energy per gallon treated for wastewater) does not point to the sensor drift that is the actual cause. The gap shows up only when you look at the control inputs directly, not at the outcomes they produce. The parallel is covered in more detail in the analysis of [why parallel equipment drifts apart](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts/). It also applies to intermittent aeration cycles for nitrogen removal, where DO sensor drift affects both effluent compliance and the energy savings the intermittent strategy was meant to deliver: [intermittent aeration for nitrogen removal: what DO sensor precision actually controls](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/intermittent-aeration-nitrogen-removal-do-control/).

## The California compliance context

California's AB 2619, signed in September 2026, requires data center operators to report total and direct annual water use by source at every business license renewal, under penalty of perjury. AB 2469 requires a Water Scarcity Plan by 2028 for facilities requiring construction permits. ([California data center water reporting requirements](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/california-data-center-water-reporting.html))

A Water Scarcity Plan is a commitment to reduce water consumption under specified drought conditions, including staged curtailment and targeted reductions by use type. The commitment is credible only if the site can demonstrate that it knows where its water goes and can reduce specific uses on demand.

A site operating at three cycles of concentration because its conductivity sensors drift between maintenance intervals cannot reliably commit to operating at six cycles under drought conditions. The chemistry that makes six cycles safe to operate requires measurement quality that makes four and a half cycles the actual operational average. The gap between the plan and the operational reality is a sensor reliability problem, not a strategy problem.

## Three questions worth checking before setting a WUE target

Before writing a WUE improvement target into a sustainability report or a Water Scarcity Plan, three questions are worth answering from existing historian data.

**What are your actual cycles of concentration, by tower?** This is calculable from makeup flow, blowdown flow, and conductivity readings. If the number is consistently below design, the control logic or the sensor driving it is worth examining before adjusting targets.

**How does blowdown volume correlate with wet-bulb temperature?** Evaporation tracks ambient conditions predictably. Blowdown should not spike independently of heat load. Unexplained blowdown events in the historian are almost always sensor artifacts or valve events, not chemistry responses.

**What share of total water use does blowdown represent?** If blowdown is running above 30 percent of total consumption on a facility that should be operating at moderate cycles, the conductivity control system is not performing at design. This shows up in 12 months of metered data and does not require a new study to identify.

None of this analysis requires capital investment. The data exists in most historian systems. The constraint is usually having a way to look at it with enough resolution and the right reference points to distinguish signal from noise.

---

If your site is preparing for California's 2027 renewal requirements or developing a scarcity plan for 2028, the water balance question is worth addressing before the commitment is made, not after. AquaMesh can review the historian data that is already being collected and identify where the measurement gaps are.

See how this kind of analysis surfaced a $3,300 per year blower anomaly at a wastewater treatment plant: [what 25 days of historian data actually shows](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows/). Or [reach out to schedule a working session](https://aquamesh.ai/#contact).

==============================================================================
TITLE: Aeration energy at wastewater plants: the cost, the waste, and the measurement gap
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/aeration-energy-cost-wastewater-plants.html
DATE: 2026-10-21
SECTION: Field notes
TAGS: aeration energy, wastewater treatment, dissolved oxygen, blower control, energy optimization
==============================================================================

Aeration is the single largest line on the electricity bill for most activated sludge wastewater plants. Aeration systems typically represent 50 to 75 percent of total electricity consumption at activated sludge facilities. The logical response is to install dissolved oxygen sensors, add variable frequency drives to blowers, and let a control loop do the rest. Many plants have done exactly that. Not all of them kept the savings.

Here is what the cost actually looks like, and why the measurement behind the control loop determines whether the savings are real and lasting.

## How large the prize is

The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported the national average industrial electricity rate at $0.0977 per kWh in July 2026, up from $0.0933 the prior year. ([EIA Electric Power Monthly, September 2026](https://www.eia.gov/electricity/monthly/epm_table_grapher.php?t=epmt_5_6_a))

Secondary treatment activated sludge plants typically use between 1,200 and 1,800 kWh per million gallons treated. The EPA's water and wastewater energy management documentation cites a common benchmark near 1,500 kWh per million gallons for secondary treatment. ([U.S. EPA, Ensuring a Sustainable Future: An Energy Management Guidebook for Wastewater and Water Utilities](https://www.epa.gov/sites/default/files/2016-12/documents/guide_energymanagement.pdf))

**Modelled example for a 10 MGD secondary treatment plant:**

| | |
|---|---|
| Annual flow treated | 3,650 million gallons |
| Electricity at 1,500 kWh/MG | 5,475,000 kWh |
| Aeration share at 60% | 3,285,000 kWh |
| At $0.098/kWh industrial rate | $321,900/year |

This is a modelled example based on published benchmarks. Actual costs vary with load patterns, treatment configuration, equipment age, and the utility tariff in effect. The kilowatt-hours are the right order of magnitude; the dollar figure resolves once you pull an actual utility bill.

At this scale, a 20 percent reduction in blower energy is worth roughly $64,000 per year. The Florida Water and Pollution Control Operators Association published analysis in April 2026 showing that basic demand-based DO control typically reduces blower energy by 10 to 25 percent, and that PLC-optimized control can reach 20 to 40 percent. ([FWPCOA, "Demand-Based DO Control And Energy Optimization," April 2026](https://www.fwpcoa.org/content.aspx?page_id=5&club_id=859275&item_id=134074))

Those are compelling numbers. The problem is that they describe what the system saves when it is working as designed. The gap between the theoretical savings and what a plant actually captures and keeps is usually a measurement problem.

## Where the savings go

A DO control loop has three components: a sensor reporting the current dissolved oxygen level, a controller comparing that reading to a setpoint, and a variable frequency drive adjusting blower output. The logic is straightforward.

The sensor is the weak link.

Electrochemical membranes foul and require regular replacement. Optical sensors are more stable but still accumulate biofilm in mixed liquor. A sensor that reads 1.8 mg/L when the actual basin concentration is 3.2 mg/L signals the controller that the basin is under-oxygenated. The controller responds by running blowers harder. The plant pays for electricity that achieves nothing useful, and nothing in the system indicates anything is wrong.

The inverse failure is less common but more consequential: a sensor fouled in a way that reads artificially high causes the controller to back off blowers when DO is genuinely borderline, with the process instability that follows.

Both failure modes are silent. The control loop is running. No alarms fire. The historian records the sensor output without knowing it has drifted. Operators checking the dashboard see normal-looking DO values.

This is why many plants install DO control hardware and see strong early results followed by gradual erosion. The hardware is still there. The control loop is still active. But the measurement feeding it has drifted, and the loop is now optimizing against a wrong input.

## The parallel basin case

Plants with multiple aeration basins running in parallel face a compounding version of this problem. Sensors in different basins drift at different rates depending on local solids loading, position relative to diffusers, and how consistently each one gets cleaned. The basins may share a common air header, but if their DO sensors are reading different offsets, the blower outputs serving them will diverge in ways that reflect sensor drift rather than actual process differences.

We covered the mechanics and cost of this kind of hidden divergence in [why parallel equipment drifts apart](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/why-parallel-equipment-drifts/). The direct energy cost of an over-aerated basin shows up in blower runtime. The downstream cost in nitrogen removal performance, when an anoxic zone receives excess dissolved oxygen, is harder to price but real.

## What the historian data showed

When we analyzed 25 days of historian data from an operating plant earlier this year, one of the first findings was a DO-driven blower anomaly: one basin was running at more than three times the DO level of its parallel twin, with its blower pinned at maximum output, for the full duration of the record.

Both basins drew on the same shared air header. The control loop was functioning. The deviation was visible only by comparing the two basins side by side at hourly resolution. A daily manual grab from either basin, taken at a representative time, could easily have missed it.

The finding was worth $3,316 per year in direct blower power, plus the process risk from carrying excess oxygen into a downstream anoxic zone. It was already in the data. It just had not been looked at in this way. The full analysis is in [what 25 days of historian data actually shows about a treatment plant](https://aquamesh.ai/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows/).

## What accurate measurement changes

When DO measurement is continuous, accurate, and does not accumulate drift between calibration cycles, the control loop has what it was designed to work from. Blower output tracks actual oxygen demand rather than sensor artifacts. Setpoints can be tightened because operators are not building in a buffer to account for measurement uncertainty.

For plants running [intermittent aeration for simultaneous nitrification/denitrification](/blog/intermittent-aeration-nitrogen-removal-do-control.html), the DO swing required is fast and narrow. The economics of that strategy depend entirely on measurement that responds quickly and without offset.

Accurate measurement also creates a defensible record of what happened. When a plant documents savings for a utility incentive program or a regulatory report, both the baseline and current performance need measurement that holds up to scrutiny.

## Three questions worth asking before tuning the control loop

Before commissioning a new aeration control strategy or investigating why existing savings have eroded, three questions are worth answering directly from available data.

**Are the DO sensors reading accurately?** A comparison between sensor output and a calibrated handheld grab at different times of day, not just right after calibration, shows whether a sensor is holding its reading or drifting between service intervals.

**What does the blower run-time history show?** If blowers are running at sustained high output during periods when influent flow and temperature are moderate, the measurement feeding the control loop deserves examination before changing the control logic itself.

**Are parallel basins loading evenly?** Persistent divergence in blower output between basins handling equivalent loads is almost always a measurement issue. It rarely responds to setpoint adjustments alone.

None of these analyses requires new hardware. The data is usually in the historian. The constraint is having a way to look at it at the right resolution, over a long enough window, against the right reference.

---

If your plant is spending in the range described above, the measurement question is worth examining directly. An initial review of your historian data can show whether the control loop is working from accurate inputs and where the largest gaps are.

See how AquaMesh approached this analysis at a membrane bioreactor reuse plant: [a membrane-bioreactor water reuse plant case study](https://aquamesh.ai/case-studies/water-reuse-plant.html). Or [reach out to schedule a working session with the team](https://aquamesh.ai/#contact).

*Alex Towfigh is a founder at AquaMesh.*


==============================================================================
TITLE: In Dairy Foods: why dairy plants still miss their most expensive process losses
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/dairy-foods-process-losses.html
DATE: 2026-10-12
SECTION: In the press
TAGS: dairy, product loss, CIP, spectral sensing, process water, Dairy Foods
==============================================================================

Dairy Foods published a contributed article by Alex Towfigh, AquaMesh's founder and CEO, on 12 October 2026. The full piece is on the Dairy Foods site: [Why dairy plants still miss their most expensive process losses](https://www.dairyfoods.com/articles/99452-why-dairy-plants-still-miss-their-most-expensive-process-losses).

What follows is a short summary. The article itself is exclusive to Dairy Foods.

## The argument in brief

**The losses happen during transitions.** Published research puts routine losses of milk to sewer at 1% to 3% of the milk a plant processes. Most of it leaves during startups, interruptions, shutdowns and rinses: short windows where the pipe contents change and someone has to decide where product ends and water begins.

**More tags do not fix a missing measurement.** Conductivity tells you something changed, but not how much product is in the line. A flowmeter tells you how much is moving, but not what it is. Lab results come back after the decision has been made. If the plant never measured the chemistry, software running on the historian has nothing to analyze.

**Spectral sensing helps, if it can be trusted.** An optical spectrum carries far more information than a single-variable sensor. But temperature, bubbles, solids and a fouled window all move the reading. Without local calibration, a dirty window can look like a product loss, so every reading needs a confidence level attached.

**Context decides what a signal means.** Rising conductivity is expected during caustic circulation and alarming during a product transfer. The article describes starting from data the plant already has (CIP steps, valve positions, lab results) to establish operating state, adding sensing only where a real blind spot exists, and producing an explanation of what changed and why rather than another generic alarm.

**Prove it one event at a time.** Start read-only. Existing controls and sanitation checks stay in charge. Pick one expensive event, measure its baseline, catch it earlier, change the decision, and verify the result. One peer-reviewed UHT cleaning study cited in the piece used phase-endpoint measurement to cut a cleaning sequence from 142 to 66 minutes and roughly halve its effluent.

The article's dollar figures are sensitivity calculations at an illustrative plant scale, not measured results at any named facility. It says so, and so do we.

[Read the full article in Dairy Foods](https://www.dairyfoods.com/articles/99452-why-dairy-plants-still-miss-their-most-expensive-process-losses).


==============================================================================
TITLE: California now asks data centers what they actually use, under penalty of perjury
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/california-data-center-water-reporting.html
DATE: 2026-10-01
SECTION: Regulation
TAGS: data centers, water reporting, AB 2619, AB 2469, cooling water, water reuse, California
==============================================================================

On 21 September 2026 the Governor of California signed [AB 2619](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB2619), now Chapter 437 of the 2026 Statutes, and [AB 2469](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB2469) alongside it. Between them they change what a data center operator in California has to be able to say about water, and when.

The reporting obligation is the part worth reading closely, because it is more specific than the coverage suggests.

## What AB 2619 actually asks for

AB 2619 works through the business license process rather than through a new permit. It sorts data centers into three types: Type I, or hyperscale, at more than 10,000 servers or more than 25 megawatts; Type II between 2 and 25 megawatts; and Type III below 2 megawatts.

At initial application, the operator gives the water supplier, and repeats on the license application form, a good faith estimate of expected water use, the anticipated source, and projected volume for the maximum day, the maximum month, and the average year.

At every renewal, the operator reports the preceding calendar year's annual water use — and here the statute is precise — "including total water use and direct water use," along with the cooling system type.

Direct annual water use is defined in the bill as:

> The volume of water withdrawn, delivered, or otherwise used onsite for data center operations, including cooling, sanitation, irrigation, and any other operational use, identified by source, including potable water, nonpotable water, or recycled water.

All of it under penalty of perjury.

Two things in that definition do the work. The first is *identified by source* — potable, nonpotable, recycled, broken out, not aggregated. The second is the split between total and direct, which means a single number off the utility bill does not satisfy the renewal requirement.

One correction worth making, because it has circulated widely: several summaries describe AB 2619 as requiring disclosure of *indirect* water use, meaning the water consumed generating the site's electricity. The enacted text does not define indirect use and does not require it. If you are scoping a compliance programme, scope it to what the statute says.

## What AB 2469 adds, and the 2028 date

AB 2469 operates on the other side of the counter. It applies to cities and counties approving discretionary or ministerial permits for data center construction or expansion that increases maximum peak water use, and it requires a Water Supply Assessment under [Water Code section 10910 et seq.](https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/codes_displayText.xhtml?lawCode=WAT&division=6.&title=&part=2.10.&chapter=&article=), projected water use and efficiency measures, workforce disclosures, and an undertaking that the applicant carries the full cost of any water conveyance, treatment, storage or distribution infrastructure the project needs.

Effective 1 January 2028, it also requires a Water Scarcity Plan. That plan has to set out measures for five named conditions — an abnormally dry year, and moderate, severe, extreme and exceptional drought years — including staged reductions, curtailment, recycling and reuse, thermal load reductions, and load shedding.

AB 2469 does not mandate closed-loop cooling. Some coverage says it does. It does not.

## The gap this opens

A Water Scarcity Plan is a commitment to cut consumption by a stated amount under stated conditions, written down in advance, in front of a permitting authority. Writing a credible one requires knowing two things that many sites do not currently know with any precision.

The first is where the water is going now, by loop and by source. Evaporative cooling, blowdown, makeup, sanitation and irrigation are different lines with different elasticities, and a site that only knows its total has no basis for saying which it would cut first.

The second is how far each one can be cut before something else breaks. Curtailment on a cooling tower usually means running at higher cycles of concentration — less blowdown, less makeup, and a circuit that is now closer to the scaling and corrosion limits of its own chemistry. Recycling and reuse, both named in the statute, move in the same direction. The water you keep in the loop is water whose composition is drifting.

That is the real operational content of a scarcity plan. It is not a reporting exercise, it is a commitment to run the plant closer to its limits on demand, and the plan is only as good as the site's ability to see what happens when it does.

## Where measurement earns its place

Volumes are a flow metering problem, and the renewal report in AB 2619 is largely a question of whether a site is instrumented well enough to break its own consumption apart by source. Many are not, and 2027's renewals will be the first time that shows up with a perjury declaration attached.

Composition is a different problem, and it is the one that decides whether a curtailment commitment is safe to make. A plant running higher cycles, or taking a recycled source that was not in the original design basis, is operating a water chemistry that moves. [Spectral change analysis](/blog/spectral-change-analysis-vs-calibrated-parameters.html) is a reasonable fit here precisely because it does not depend on having a calibrated panel for every constituent that might matter — it watches the spectrum for what is correlating with something the operator cares about, and flags when that relationship moves. BOD is the one parameter AquaMesh calibrates; the rest is change detection.

For sites that already have a few months of history in a historian, the first question is usually answerable from data that exists. [What 25 days of one plant's data showed](/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows.html) is a reasonable picture of what that kind of look turns up, and it was not a water reporting exercise — it was a cost exercise that happened to require knowing where things actually go.

Nothing in either bill requires a sensor. Both require a site to be able to answer questions about its own water that a surprising number of operators currently answer by estimate. The first renewals under AB 2619 will establish how much tolerance there is for that, and the 2028 scarcity plans will establish how much tolerance there is for a commitment that nobody has tested.

Operators working through what this means for an existing site can see how we approach [data center cooling water](/industries/data-centers.html), or start with an audit of the data already being collected.


==============================================================================
TITLE: What 25 days of historian data actually shows about a treatment plant
URL: https://aquamesh.ai/blog/what-25-days-of-historian-data-shows.html
DATE: 2026-09-30
SECTION: Field notes
TAGS: historian data, wastewater energy, plant audit, SCADA, membrane bioreactor
==============================================================================

A water reuse plant gave us an export of its own historian and nothing else. No site visit, no new instruments, no interviews. Twenty-five days of operation: 1,001 tags, 7,172,532 recorded values, 28 June to 23 July.

That export was enough to rank what the plant was losing, and to put an annual figure on each item. This is what the work looked like and what came out of it.

![Audit summary: about $42,050 a year in savings with no capital spend, rising to $92,200 with a later instrumentation phase; a $147,000 a year power bill; 71% of design flow; effluent turbidity 0.11 NTU.](../assets/audit/fig1.jpg "The front page of the delivered audit. Values tagged **M** are measured straight from the plant’s SCADA; **E** means we calculated them, and the assumptions are written down.")

## Why a historian export is enough to start

Almost every plant already records far more than anyone reads. A SCADA historian captures every tag on a schedule, forever, and the overwhelming majority of those tags are never looked at unless something breaks. The data is not the constraint. Attention is.

Three properties make that archive useful:

- **It is continuous.** A lab result describes one moment. A historian describes every moment, which is the only way to see a slope rather than a point.
- **It contains pairs.** Plants run parallel equipment — twin basins, duty and standby pumps, two membrane trains. Equipment built to do the same job under the same conditions should behave the same way. When it stops, that divergence is a measurement in itself.
- **It is already paid for.** No capital request, no procurement cycle, no installation window.

## The method

For each signal we model what normal looks like for that signal at that plant, rather than against a textbook range. Where the plant publishes its own operating ranges — most do, on the weekly sampling schedule — those become the reference. A finding only counts as a finding if it sits outside the range the plant itself posts.

Then each item is priced, which is the part that decides whether anyone acts:

- Blower power from the isentropic relation, using measured airflow and measured discharge pressure
- Pump power from measured flow and head
- Runtime from historian totaliser deltas
- Everything converted to money using the plant's own tariff

Each line is labelled **measured** or **estimated**. Where it is an estimate, the assumptions are written down so the plant's own engineer can check the arithmetic rather than take a vendor's word for it.

## What came out

### One basin running 3.6x above its own posted range

The plant's sampling schedule posts pre-air dissolved oxygen at 0.5–1.5 mg/L. Basin 2 sat right in that band, median 0.49 mg/L. Basin 1 held a median of 5.35 mg/L on every day of the record — roughly eleven times its twin — with its blower command pinned at 99.99%.

Both basins draw on the same shared air header. That detail is what turns this from a mystery into a maintenance task: if the air supply is common and the outcomes are not, the problem is in the split — a valve or a damper — not in the control strategy. Worth $3,316 a year in blower power, plus the nitrogen-removal risk of carrying that much oxygen into an anoxic zone.

{{diagram:twin-basins}} — Both basins draw on the same air header, so the difference is in the split rather than the control strategy.

One caveat we put in the report and will repeat here: a fouled DO probe can sit on an offset and still respond to airflow. The reading gets verified against a calibrated handheld before anyone opens a valve.

### Membrane scour air above what the flux needed

Airflow tracked the permeate rate almost perfectly — R² of 1.00 — at a ratio well above the manufacturer's specific-scour guidance. Trimming toward the guideline at the measured flux, using the controls already installed, came to $5,391 a year. That was the largest no-capital line on the list.

### Pumps starting every twenty-five seconds

Reclaimed water pumps were logging 13 to 28 starts an hour against a manufacturer guideline near six for pumps that size. One asset logged 143 in an hour — a start every twenty-five seconds.

Every start draws locked-rotor current and heats the windings far more than running does. This is a control deadband, not a purchase, and it was quietly writing a bill in motors, starters and contactors: about $3,500 a year.

### Sixteen of sixteen reuse totalisers frozen

Every irrigation zone has a volume totaliser. Not one of them changed in twenty-five days.

Until they record, nobody can demonstrate how much recycled water went to beneficial reuse rather than straight to disposal — which is exactly the number a reuse programme is judged on. A configuration fix rather than a purchase, and it unlocks roughly $7,300 a year.

## What it added up to

| | |
|---|---|
| Direct savings, no capital at all | **$42,050 / yr** |
| Including ~7 h/week of reporting time returned | **$58,428 / yr** |
| Fully instrumented, direct | **$75,800 / yr** |
| Fully instrumented, all in | **$92,200 / yr** |

Two subtotals are kept deliberately apart: money that comes off a bill, and operator hours given back. The hours are real, but they are not money off a bill, so they never get folded into the first number.

![Opportunity table with every line flagged measured or estimated: pre-air basin oxygen correction $3,316 measured; modulating pre-air control $1,718 estimated; RAS flow optimisation $1,096 estimated; predictive maintenance programme $20,900 estimated; direct savings subtotal $42,048; reporting automation $16,380 estimated; everything added up $58,428.](../assets/audit/fig2.jpg "Every line labelled. The predictive-maintenance figure is built asset by asset from the plant’s own run hours and start counts, not taken as a percentage of a maintenance budget.")

## The caveat that matters most

Everything above is priced on a residential time-of-use schedule blending to $0.362/kWh. At 406,610 kWh a year this plant is well past residential scale and would normally sit on a commercial schedule at roughly half that blended rate.

On a commercial tariff, the same physical savings are worth about half what is shown.

The kilowatt-hours are measured either way; only their price is in question, and one utility bill settles it. We put that on the front page of the report rather than in a footnote, because showing the range is worth more than picking the flattering end of it.

## What this does not tell you

A twenty-five day window in summer will not capture seasonal variation. Capital figures other than instrumentation are order-of-magnitude and need firming with quotes. And every number here is a **ceiling** that assumes the recommendation is actually implemented and then maintained — an identified opportunity, not a realised saving.

![The AquaMesh recommendations view: findings with severity, the action to take, the evidence tags and the annual value, with accept, resolve and dismiss on each card.](../assets/audit.jpg "The same findings in the platform, where they keep recomputing on a rolling window rather than ageing in a PDF. Plant name removed; everything else is the product as it ships.")

If your plant keeps a historian, the same exercise is available on your data. It needs an export and nothing else.

Read the full anonymised audit: [a membrane-bioreactor water reuse plant](/case-studies/water-reuse-plant.html).

## What it covers

**The problem.** Many plants still find critical problems through delayed lab tests, manual checks, indirect measurements, or alarms that only fire after the problem has already formed. Unplanned industrial downtime is estimated to cost about $260,000 an hour on average.

Where a physical or chemical condition can't be measured any other way, it adds its own sensing. Closing it pays off now through production, downtime and operating cost. Over the longer term it is the foundation for facilities that optimize themselves, starting with information operators can trust.
